notes:
I've put together notes on Job 34. The main sources I read in full are Enduring Word (David Guzik) and the Pulpit Commentary. I added material from Matthew Henry, Coffman, John Wesley and Desiring God (John Piper and Christopher Ash), mostly taken from search-result excerpts.

There are gaps. I didn't get to Gill's or Ellicott's notes on each verse; the only Ellicott I saw is on v. 1. I found nothing for Job 34 on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The Wesley page I opened cut off before chapter 34, so I only have his note on v. 34.

**The issue behind the whole chapter: is Elihu right?**
How a teacher reads Job 34 depends mostly on what he thinks of Elihu. That splits teachers more than the denominations do.
- **Calvary Chapel (Guzik):** Elihu gets Job's words wrong, quoting him "selectively and unfairly." He then defends God's justice with truths that are right in themselves but don't speak to Job's actual suffering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/
- **Baptist (Piper):** Piper treats Elihu's speech as "a preliminary word from God" before God speaks, and notes that God rebukes the three friends but not Elihu (42:7). https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-the-young-speak In another sermon he says Elihu's words are true and prepare the way for God's final word. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-rebuked-in-suffering
- **Reformed (Calvin, as reported by Christopher Ash):** Calvin has nothing negative to say about Elihu and admires him as speaking like "a true doctor of the church." Ash himself came to see Elihu as a true prophet. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak
- **Methodist (Wesley):** On 42:7, Wesley says Elihu isn't rebuked because he was more merciful to Job: he condemned Job's "sinful expressions" but not Job himself. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xix.xliii.ii.html
- **Restoration (Coffman):** Coffman says Elihu repeats the three friends' errors and is even harsher toward Job. He denies that Elihu introduces God's speech. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-37.html
- **Catholic tradition (as reported by Ash):** Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas both treat Elihu's teaching as orthodox. Both still criticise his motives as proud or seeking empty glory. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak
- **Modern scholarship (as described by Ash):** Ash says scholars today almost all treat Elihu as unorthodox, like the other friends. Some argue his speeches were added to the book later. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak

**Verse by verse**

v. 1: Ellicott says Elihu immediately starts accusing Job, which doesn't match his claim to be wise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/34-1.htm Gill pictures Elihu pausing to see whether Job would reply before going on. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/34-1.htm

v. 2: The Pulpit Commentary says it's unclear whether the "wise men" are the three friends or a wider crowd. It also notes that talking about Job's conduct in front of him was hardly polite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman notes the crowd is only imagined; the text never mentions one. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/job-34.html Matthew Henry notes Elihu still calls men he disagrees with wise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_034.cfm

v. 3: This is a proverb Job himself had already used (12:11). Its point is that the ear should sort good words from bad as the palate sorts food. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 4: The Pulpit Commentary calls this a call to reach a right verdict together. The sentiment is good but somewhat pompous from a young man speaking to his elders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 5: The Pulpit Commentary says Job defended his integrity but never claimed to be sinless. He also never said "I am righteous" in so many words; the closest is 13:18. When Job said God had taken away his justice (27:2), he meant God was withholding a verdict, not perverting one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 6: Job refused to confess sins he wasn't aware of, because that would be lying about his own case. The Pulpit Commentary says he didn't sin in this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik says Job claimed no special sin behind his disaster, not sinlessness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

v. 7: The Pulpit Commentary calls the jab unnecessary and unfair. Job hadn't scorned God, and the friends had earned whatever scorn he gave them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman cites Keil that "scoffing" carries the sense of blasphemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-34.html

v. 8: The Pulpit Commentary says Elihu here accuses Job of joining the ungodly (Ps 1:1), which grossly exaggerates Job's faults. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik thinks Elihu more likely meant that Job's confused thinking put him alongside the wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

v. 9: The Pulpit Commentary says Job never said this. The nearest is 9:22, and elsewhere Job was speaking of his own case and his deep confusion about it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman says nothing Job said justifies this charge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-34.html

v. 10: The Pulpit Commentary says a God who does wrong is a contradiction in terms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Henry: God cannot do wickedness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/job-34.html

v. 11:
- The Pulpit Commentary says God repays people according to their whole conduct (Ps 62:13). The exactness can't be seen in this life but will be at the end. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html
- Guzik says Elihu repeats Eliphaz's "you reap what you sow" formula. He warns against treating Galatians 6:7 as a law of "spiritual karma." Applied absolutely, that law "would surely damn us all." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/
- Coffman says Elihu talks a lot about God's justice and not at all about grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-34.html

v. 12: The Pulpit Commentary finds nothing new here beyond v. 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik says Elihu is right, but he assumes God never acts mysteriously. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

v. 13: The Pulpit Commentary reads it this way: nobody delegated God's authority, so he has no interest separate from his creatures and no temptation to be unjust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Constable calls the idea that God answers to no one "the edge of a dangerous cliff." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/34-10.html

vv. 14–15:
- The Pulpit Commentary gives two readings of whose "spirit and breath" is meant, God's own or man's. Either way, God could reduce humanity to nothing, so he has no need to treat anyone unjustly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html
- Benson (quoted on Bible Hub) says God would only need to withdraw his preserving power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/34-1.htm
- Guzik says the point is God's independence and transcendence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

v. 16: The Pulpit Commentary thinks this appeal is to any wise listener, not Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Henry instead reads it as Elihu appealing directly to Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/job-34.html

v. 17: The Pulpit Commentary compares it to Abraham's "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik calls it unfair to treat Job's anguish as condemning God, since Job loved God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

vv. 18–19: The Pulpit Commentary follows the KJV wording ("Is it fit to say to a king…?"). It reasons that if no one would accuse an earthly king, still less should anyone accuse God, who doesn't favour princes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman says the argument fails because fools do sometimes hold high office. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-34.html

v. 20: The Pulpit Commentary links this to the Passover night (Ex 12:29) and Daniel 2:34. "Without hand" means without human agency. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman thinks Elihu was hinting at Job's own expected death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-34.html

v. 21: Because God knows everything, he can weigh exactly what each person is due. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 22: Darkness hides nothing from God (Heb 4:13; Ps 139). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 23: Following the Revised Version, the Pulpit Commentary takes it to mean God needs no second hearing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman notes this answers Job's wish for an umpire. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-34.html

v. 24: The Pulpit Commentary prefers "in ways past finding out" to "without number." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Coffman says everyone listening knew Elihu meant Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-34.html

vv. 25–27: God's judgments fall suddenly and publicly, as an example to others. Turning back from God is a sin (Prov 1:24–32). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik reads this as a warning aimed at Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

v. 28: God hears the oppressed and punishes their oppressors (Ex 22:23). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik retells a story from Adam Clarke: a Scottish landowner who was persecuting poor believers left them alone after they threatened to pray against him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/ The Restoration Commentary says implying Job oppressed the poor is the opposite of the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/job-34.html

v. 29: The Pulpit Commentary compares it to Romans 8:31–34. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Bridgeway says no one can force God to explain himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/34-10.html

v. 30: The Pulpit Commentary calls the Hebrew obscure. Its preferred sense is that God removes ungodly rulers so they stop harming people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik quotes Andersen: if everything that happens is right by definition, "the category of evil disappears." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

vv. 31–32: The Pulpit Commentary gives two readings, advice to Job to submit or a question. It slightly prefers the question. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik takes these as the words Elihu thinks Job should have said. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/ Henry says Elihu only asks Job to admit he spoke rashly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_034.cfm

v. 33: Should God judge as Job thinks right? The choice is Job's to make. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik notes Elihu uses ultimatums the friends didn't. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

vv. 28–33 (text problem): Coffman, citing other scholars, says these verses are very difficult and were left out of the Greek Old Testament. He quotes Driver calling them "unintelligible, or at least very ambiguous." https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/job-34.html

v. 34: Wesley paraphrases Elihu as content to let any wise man judge his words. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/

v. 35: The words Elihu means are the ones that seemed to accuse God of injustice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html

v. 36: The Pulpit Commentary reads "tested" as gold is tested. It notes the irony that Elihu got his wish: God's final verdict was that Job had spoken rightly (42:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html Guzik says Elihu's compassion had worn thin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/ Coffman reads it as "confess or die." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-34.html

v. 37:
- The Pulpit Commentary takes clapping as Job applauding himself instead of repenting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-34.html
- Bible Hub's notes instead call it a gesture of scorn (Nahum 3:19). https://biblehub.com/job/34.htm
- Guzik takes it as Job scorning his friends' advice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/

**Popular modern teaching:** None of the sources named prosperity or word-of-faith teaching directly. Guzik's warning at v. 11, against treating "reap what you sow" as an absolute spiritual law, is the closest thing I found. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-34/
